text.p: Wool prices have declined to the point where no one in the industry is making profits, John Ring, managing director of Wesfarmers Dalgety Ltd, said on Monday.

"Prices are so low no one's making money in this business," Ring said in an interview. He said international and Australian prices were being driven soley by supply, a situation that must be reversed to take into account demand if prices were to rise.
Wool faces mounting competition from substitutes and a move away from woollen clothing by younger consumers. "Young people just aren't buying that many (wool) suits anymore," Ring said.

While current production of wool in Australia, the highest in the world, is only about half the bumper clip of 1990, current stockpiles will take until 2000 to deplete under an existing draw down programme, Ring said.

Ring said the auction system of wool sales in Australia -- accounting for about 95 percent of all sales -- was outdated in the absence of an active forward market, a concept not fully grasped by some 60 percent of Australia's estimated 60,000 wool growers.
"They must recognise that this is the future of the industry," he said.
Earlier on Monday, Wesfarmers Dalgety and rival Elders Australia Ltd predicted a proposed joint venture designed to promote a forward market in Australia would be launched July 1.
The joint venture would be capitalised at around A$100 million, with Wesfarmers Dalgety and Elders contributing about A$33 million each and growers supplying the remaining one-third.
The funds could be generated through a combination of debt and equity, Ring said.
